captions.text: For two loop readings, yes. Here the order costs you a sign.

videos.title: A Cup of Counterexample
videos.plays: Before World 3 · Level 4, at the Twin Islands
videos.synopsis: Null's torus and bouquet-with-sphere share every hole count. The Cup Caster lights the top class on one and not the other.

scenes.title: Twins
scenes.description: The torus and the bouquet; both meters read ℤ, ℤ², ℤ.

scenes.title: Cast on the torus
scenes.description: α ⌣ β on the torus: the top lantern blazes.

scenes.title: Cast on the bouquet
scenes.description: The beams light separate rings; the ball stays dark.

scenes.title: Side by side
scenes.description: One lantern lit, one dark.

scenes.title: Title
scenes.description: Title card: World 3 · Level 4 · A Cup of Counterexample.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: The twins. The torus is going grey at the edges… but that window’s still lit.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: On the torus, the two loop readings multiply to the top class.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: On the bouquet they never meet. Nothing lights.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Different products, different places. Light it, Gyroid.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: One lit, one dark. Hang on in there, whoever you are. You’re staying.

videos.title: Product Placement
videos.plays: Before World 3 · Level 5
videos.synopsis: In the Parterre, rows times columns: a product's readings come from its factors.

scenes.title: The grid
scenes.description: A grid garden: rows and columns of beds for S¹ × S¹.

scenes.title: Crossings
scenes.description: Each bed goes to its degree bin: 1, 2, 1 — the torus.

scenes.title: Title
scenes.description: Title card: World 3 · Level 5 · Product Placement.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A point of a product is a pair of points, so its readings come in pairs too. Rows times columns.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Circle times circle. The torus again, still standing. Good.

videos.title: Polynomial Garden
videos.plays: Before World 3 · Level 6
videos.synopsis: On projective spaces one lantern's powers light the whole garden — then stop. Borsuk–Ulam follows.

scenes.title: The fountain
scenes.description: The ℝP⁴ fountain with α lit.

scenes.title: Powers
scenes.description: Gyroid casts α again and again: α², α³, α⁴ — then α⁵ fizzles.

scenes.title: Antipodes
scenes.description: ℝP⁴ and ℝP² climbed together: α³ lights one and fizzles on the other.

scenes.title: Title
scenes.description: Title card: World 3 · Level 6 · Polynomial Garden.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In this garden, one class makes all the others, just by multiplying itself.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Square, cube… right to the top. And then nothing.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: That stopping point is why some maps can’t exist. There are things not even the Crown can make.

videos.title: Which Way Is Up
videos.plays: Before World 3 · Level 7, at the Compass Cliffs
videos.synopsis: On Poincaré Reach, compasses must agree everywhere — unless the land is twisted. Each place has a two-sheeted orientation cover.

scenes.title: The cliffs
scenes.description: A band of six patches with a half-twisted seam.

scenes.title: Compasses

videos.title: How the Tide Works
videos.plays: After the 0-2 intro, before play starts; replayable from the level's “How it works” button
videos.synopsis: A slowed-down explainer of 0-2's idea and tools. A path is a map f : I → X; a homotopy is a continuous movie of paths, one map F on the square I × I whose rows are the frames fₜ; rel A means the posts never move (the square's side edges). The Tide Glass scrubs t; the Spool makes homotopies by hand and hooks the ribbon onto stakes. What breaks a homotopy: a cut, a jump between frames, crossing water. A 3D demo on the flats plays beside a 2D diagram of the interval and the square.

scenes.title: A path is a map
scenes.description: Top-down over a ribbon between two posts. A bead slides along the ribbon while, in the diagram, a bead slides along the interval [0, 1]: s ↦ f(s).

scenes.title: A homotopy is a movie
scenes.description: The tide bends the ribbon from t = 0 to t = 1; five frames freeze as ghosts. The diagram becomes the square I × I, each frozen frame a row, the current frame a gold row at height t.

scenes.title: The Tide Glass
scenes.description: The movie scrubs back and forth; the diagram shows the Tide Glass slider and Z / X keys, and faint ghosts hug the ribbon on either side.

scenes.title: Rel A
scenes.description: The two posts pulse gold; the square's left and right edges light up: F(0, t) = a, F(1, t) = b for every t — the ribbon's ends are pinned (A).

scenes.title: The Spool
scenes.description: Gyroid walks to the ribbon, clicks to grab it, walks it out to a stake and clicks to let go; it hooks on. The diagram lights each control as it's used.

scenes.title: What breaks a homotopy
scenes.description: Three forbidden moves: a cut (the ribbon in two pieces, violet sparks), a jump (two neighbouring frames far apart), and crossing water at the pool shrine (the wet stretch violet).

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Crane up over the flats; the diagram shows the summary card. Title card at 65.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Let’s slow everything down. This gold ribbon is a path: a map $f$ from the interval $I = [0, 1]$ into the flats.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Slide $s$ from 0 to 1, and $f(s)$ runs along the ribbon from one post to the other.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now let the tide move it. At each time $t$ there’s a new path, $fₜ$. Here are a few frames.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Stack every frame and you get one map $F(s, t)$ on the square $I × I$: $s$ along the ribbon, $t$ through time. Each row of the square is one frame.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So a homotopy is the whole movie — not just the first and last picture.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The Tide Glass scrubs that movie. Press 3 to hold it; Z and X — or the wheel — move $t$ back and forth.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Watch the faint ghosts either side: in a real homotopy, neighbouring frames are always close together.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: And the posts? The ribbon’s ends never move, in any frame: $F(0, t) = a$ and $F(1, t) = b$ for every $t$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: That’s a homotopy relative to $A$ — $rel A$ — where $A$ is the set of points on the ribbon that are pinned in place.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Your Spool makes homotopies by hand. Press 2, walk up to the ribbon and click to grab it.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Walk, and the ribbon follows. Every step is a new frame, so the movie stays continuous.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Click beside a stake to let go: the ribbon hooks on, and that point joins $A$ — one more point that stays put.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Three things break a homotopy. A cut: the ribbon has to stay in one piece.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A jump: no frame can leap away from the one before.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: And crossing water: every frame has to stay on the flats.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So: a homotopy is a continuous movie of paths, and $rel A$ means the pinned points stay put. That’s all the shrines ask.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Bend, don’t break. Got it.

captions.text: Two reefs: a figure-eight and a theta. They look different. Are they the same shape?

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In topology, “same shape” means something precise — maps both ways that can be undone, up to sliding.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Start with a map f from the eight to the theta: each loop of the eight goes once around one loop of the theta.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary

captions.text: This reef deforms onto the eight… and onto the theta. Same shape.

scenes.title: At the furnace
scenes.description: Gyroid steps onto a furnace, clicks to forge the point, walks the track out and back to forge edge a, walks it again to write a, and clicks to press a disk along a (a hemisphere folds above the press).

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: The torus again; the summary card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Everything in the Foundry is built in stages. First, points — the 0-cells.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Then edges, glued on by their two ends. Glue both ends to the same point and the edge becomes a loop.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Then disks, glued along loops. Each stage sits inside the next.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The simplest sphere: one point, and one disk whose entire rim is crushed onto that point.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Like pulling the drawstring on a bag until the opening's gone.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The torus: one point, two loops $a$ and $b$, and one square disk. Its rim is glued along $a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Watch matching arrows meet: the two a-sides glue into a tube, then the two b-sides bend the tube round into a ring.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now one loop, $a$, and a disk whose rim goes round $a$ twice — the same way both times.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: There’s no room in our space to do that without the disk passing through itself. That’s the projective plane.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: And a count: points minus edges plus disks. That’s χ, the Euler characteristic.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Build the same place two different ways and χ comes out the same — though proving that waits for World 2.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Here's how it works at a furnace. Watch Gyroid.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Click the furnace with the Cell-Smith: that's the point.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Walk out along the track, round its loop and back onto the furnace: an edge, $a$ — a loop at the point.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Walk it again, the way its arrows point. That writes $a$ on the disk's rim — see “walked” on the panel.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Then click the furnace: the press glues a disk along $a$. A bowl — a hemisphere.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: And lash the Unglues — if one tears an edge, walk that track again.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Points, edges, disks. Let's build.

videos.title: New Spaces from Old
videos.plays: After the 0-5 intro, before play starts; replayable from the level's “How it works” button
videos.synopsis: Operations on spaces, slowly: the cone (a ring's hole fills and every loop slides to the tip); the suspension (two points → a circle → a sphere); the wedge (two rings touch at one point); the product (a small ring swept round a big one: a torus, with a cell for each pair of cells); the quotient (a disk's rim collapsed: a sphere); then the works' controls.

scenes.title: The cone
scenes.description: A glowing ring; its tip rises and pulls it into a cone. A loop on the rim slides up the cone and vanishes at the tip. Diagram: CX, X's cells plus one on each plus the tip; χ = 1.

scenes.title: The suspension
scenes.description: Two points sprout arcs to a tip above and below: a circle. The circle grows a double cone that rounds into a sphere. Diagram: S(S⁰) = S¹, S(S¹) = S².

scenes.title: The wedge
scenes.description: Two rings glide together until they touch at one point: a figure-eight. Diagram: X ∨ Y, cells add, minus one point.

scenes.title: The product
scenes.description: A small ring travels round a big one, sweeping out a torus. Diagram: the four pairs of cells, 1 + 2 + 1.

scenes.title: The quotient
scenes.description: A disk's rim is drawn to one point and it closes into a sphere. Diagram: D²/∂D² = S²; collapsing something contractible keeps the shape.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The works' controls: pick up, feed, choose the operation, take the result off the shelf, pull plugs.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Cone, suspension, wedge, product, quotient — and the cells each adds.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A cone: take a space and join every one of its points to a single new tip.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Cone a ring and the hole fills in. Any loop on it can slide up to the tip and shrink away — a cone always shrinks to its tip.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A suspension uses two tips, one above and one below. Suspend two points and you get two arcs: a circle.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Suspend the circle and you get a double cone, which is a sphere. Each suspension climbs one dimension.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A wedge glues two spaces together at a single point. Two rings make a figure-eight.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A product: every point of one space paired with every point of the other. A ring times a ring, swept round, is a torus.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Its cells come in pairs: point with point, point with edge, edge with point, edge with edge. That's one point, two edges and one disk.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A quotient collapses part of a space to a single point. Collapse a disk's rim and it closes up into a sphere.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The rim was a loop, so the shape changed. Collapse something that shrinks to a point and the shape stays the same.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: At each works: click a pedestal to pick up a copy of its space, then click the machine to feed it in.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: New spaces land on the shelf, and you can carry them back in. Lash the Coners. If one plugs a pedestal, click it to pull the plug.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Cone, suspend, wedge, multiply, collapse. Got it.

videos.title: Felling Trees
videos.plays: After the 0-6 intro, before play starts; replayable from the level's “How it works” button
videos.synopsis: Felling trees, slowly: a tree (no cycle) has n − 1 edges and collapses to a point safely; a graph with a cycle — a triangle with a tail — gets a spanning tree marked (n − 1 edges touching every node, the edge that would close the cycle refused), and felling it leaves the unmarked edge as a loop round the surviving hole; collapsing the cycle too kills the hole; χ = nodes − edges and petals = 1 − χ; then the Spool and Cell-Smith controls. Uses both names: nodes (platforms) and edges (walkways).

scenes.title: A tree
scenes.description: A tree of 4 nodes and 3 edges. Gyroid marks each edge amber (n − 1 = 3), then fells it: every node slides into one — a point.

scenes.title: A cycle
scenes.description: A triangle with a tail: 4 nodes, 4 edges. The triangle's three edges glow pink — a cycle — round a dark disk labelled 'hole'.

scenes.title: A spanning tree
scenes.description: Gyroid marks the tail and two sides of the triangle: 3 = n − 1 edges, every node reached. He tries the third side; it flashes red, refused — it would close the cycle.

scenes.title: Fell
scenes.description: The marked tree folds into one node; the unmarked side rounds out into a loop at that node, the hole carried inside it.

scenes.title: The wrong cut
scenes.description: The same graph with all four edges marked violet, cycle included; it collapses to a point and the hole shrinks to nothing.

scenes.title: χ
scenes.description: The petal again; diagram: tree 4 − 3 = 1 → no petals, cycle 4 − 4 = 0 → one petal, petals = 1 − χ.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Spool marks edges, cycle-closing edges refused; Cell-Smith clicks any node to fell; lash Loop-biters.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Every connected graph is a bouquet of 1 − χ circles.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A graph is made of nodes — the platforms — joined by edges — the walkways. This one is a tree: it has no cycles.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A tree on $n$ nodes always has exactly $n − 1$ edges. Here: 4 nodes, 3 edges. Gyroid marks them all.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now he fells it: every edge shrinks, every node slides into one. A tree has no hole in it, so nothing is lost — it’s just a point.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: This graph has a cycle: the triangle. Follow its three edges and you come back where you started.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A cycle goes round a hole. That hole is what makes this space more than a point, and we must not lose it.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So we don’t fell everything. Gyroid marks a spanning tree: edges that reach every node, never closing a cycle. That takes $n − 1 = 3$ edges.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The third side of the triangle? Refused. Marking it would close the cycle, and a cycle isn’t a tree.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Every node is touched, no cycle is closed. That’s a spanning tree.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Fell it. The tree shrinks into one node — safe, because a tree has no hole.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The edge he didn’t mark now starts and ends at that one node: it’s a loop, a petal. The hole is still inside it.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now the wrong cut: mark every edge, the cycle too, and squash it all.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Everything goes to a point, and the hole dies with it. That’s a different space — Null’s move.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Count nodes minus edges: that’s $χ$. The tree: $4 − 3 = 1$. The cycle graph: $4 − 4 = 0$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Felling never changes $χ$, and the petals you end with number $1 − χ$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: On the decks: hold the Spool and click edges to mark a spanning tree. An edge that would close a cycle is refused.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: When the tree reaches every node, take the Cell-Smith and click any node to fell onto it. And lash those Loop-biters.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Mark a tree, keep the cycles. Timber!

videos.title: One Cell at a Time
videos.plays: After the 0-B intro; replayable from the level's “How it works” button
videos.synopsis: The homotopy extension property, slowly: X × I as space × time; A's given motion as teal columns; extending over a free point (it stays put) and an edge (it stretches between its ends); a disk refused until its whole rim moves; why it always works (Dⁿ × I retracts onto its floor and walls); controls.

scenes.title: Space × time
scenes.description: An edge on the cylinder floor; its left end's motion rises as a teal column.

scenes.title: Extend
scenes.description: The right point's column rises straight; then the edge's sheet stretches between the two columns.

scenes.title: Boundary first
scenes.description: A square with a disk: the disk is refused (its rim flashes red); points, then edges fill; then the disk's column.

scenes.title: Why it works
scenes.description: Diagram: projecting Dⁿ × I from a point above lands it on its floor and walls.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Click glowing cells; refused cells show what's missing.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Every CW pair has the homotopy extension property.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The cylinder's floor is a space, X. Going up the cylinder is time.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Part of the floor, A, already has a motion chosen for it. Here it's the left point, drifting as time goes up.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: To extend the motion, start with the free point. It only has to start in the right place, so it can just stay put.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now both ends of the edge are decided. The edge's column simply stretches between them.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A disk is different. Its column has a floor and walls, and the walls are its rim's columns. Until those are decided, it's refused.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So go in order of dimension: points, then the edges around the disk, then the disk itself.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Why does the disk's column always fill? A box, disk times time, can be squashed onto just its floor and walls.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Shine a light from a point above it: every point of the box lands on the floor or a wall.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the Cylinder Works: click a glowing cell on the floor to raise its column.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: If its boundary isn't decided yet, the missing cells flash red.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: One cell at a time. Got it.

videos.title: Covers and Lifts
videos.plays: Lesson for World 1 · Level 8 (replayable in level)
videos.synopsis: Two-sheet circle cover; wiring the figure-eight; ab closes but ba does not; Cord and Compass controls demo.

scenes.title: A two-sheeted cover
scenes.description: One loop below, two sheets above joined by a-edges; a bead runs a twice, the lift goes 1 → 2 → 1.

scenes.title: Covers of the figure-eight
scenes.description: The figure-eight below, a 3-sheet cover graph above; a bead runs a b, the lift follows.

scenes.title: The proof
scenes.description: In the cover a = (1 2 3), b = (1 2): the lift of a b closes, the lift of b a ends on sheet 3.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Gyroid runs the orange petal; his lift moves on the graph.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A covering space hangs over a space in sheets: here, two over one loop. Your lift, the white bead, copies every step you take below.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: One lap of $a$ carries the lift from sheet 1 to sheet 2. Two laps bring it back — that lift closes.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Covers of the figure-eight are graphs: one dot per sheet, and an $a$-edge and a $b$-edge in and out of every dot.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Run a word below, and the lift follows the edges with the same letters, in the same order.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now the key fact: loops that slide into each other lift to paths that end in the same place.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: $a$ then $b$: sheet 1, to 2, back to 1. It closes!

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: $b$ then $a$: sheet 1, to 2, to 3. It doesn’t!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So $a b$ and $b a$ can’t slide into each other: $ab ≠ ba$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: On the viaduct, run petals with the Winding Cord (4). The white bead above you is your lift, on its sheet.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: And the Sheet Compass (6) sets where $a$ and $b$ send each sheet — then tests $a b$ and $b a$ at the beacon.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now go and find me a cover that tells $ab$ from $ba$.

videos.title: Fixed Endpoints
videos.plays: Replay from Endpoint Gardens · ? How it works
videos.synopsis: Path homotopy rel the endpoints, slowly: a route is a path f : [0, 1] → X from gate A to gate B; a homotopy F(s, t) slides one route into another with F(0, t) = A and F(1, t) = B; a hedge splits routes into two classes (proof of that waits for 1-3); a change of pace is a homotopy; concatenation A → B → C; then the Spool, the ledger bins and the Tide Glass.

scenes.title: A route is a path
scenes.description: A garden deck with two gatehouses A and B; a bead walks the straight route between them.

scenes.title: Sliding
scenes.description: A wavy route; a teal ghost slides it onto the straight one while pink rings pin both gates.

scenes.title: A hedge
scenes.description: A hedge bed rises between an upper and a lower route; the ghost slide from upper toward lower jams against the hedge.

scenes.title: Pace
scenes.description: The upper route with a dashed copy; the bead walks it quickly — same curve, new timing.

scenes.title: Chains
scenes.description: A third gatehouse C; a route A → B and a route B → C join into one route A → C.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Gyroid picks the wavy route with the Spool (it glows white), then scrubs the Tide Glass.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: The two hedge classes; the summary card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A route is a path: a map $f$ from $[0, 1]$ into the gardens. It starts at gate $A$ and ends at gate $B$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Walk $s$ from 0 to 1 and $f(s)$ runs along the route. Many routes join the same two gates — different shapes, same ends.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Two routes are the same delivery if one slides into the other. The slide is a map $F(s, t)$: one route for each moment $t$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: And the gates never move: $F(0, t) = A$ and $F(1, t) = B$ at every moment. That’s a homotopy rel the endpoints.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now a hedge bed sits between the upper route and the lower one. Try to slide one onto the other…

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: …and the slide jams at the hedge. These two are different delivery classes. Proving that no slide can ever work takes a new tool — you’ll get it on the Winding Road.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Pace doesn’t matter. The dashed copy walks the very same curve faster. Changing the timing is a slide too, so it’s the same class.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Routes chain. A route $A → B$ followed by a route $B → C$ is a route $A → C$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: And swapping a leg for another route in its class doesn’t change the chain’s class: $[f] · [g] = [f · g]$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the gardens, hold the Spool and click a route to pick it up, then drop it in a ledger bin. Same bin, same class.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The Tide Glass scrubs a slide: hold Z and X to move $t$, and watch the ghost glide with the gates pinned.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So the route can wander all it likes, as long as both ends stay put.

videos.title: Loops at a Point
videos.plays: World 1 · Level 2 lesson

scenes.title: A loop at x₀
scenes.description: A bead runs the gold petal from the amber pad and back: f(0) = f(1) = x₀.

scenes.title: The product
scenes.description: The bead runs α then β, each at double speed: f · g.

scenes.title: Identity and inverse
scenes.description: Out along α and straight back; then f · f̄ goes out less and less far and shrinks onto the pad.

scenes.title: Associativity
scenes.description: Two beads run α β γ on the same trails: one timed (α β) γ, one α (β γ). Timing bars on the card.

scenes.title: Change of basepoint
scenes.description: A second beacon x₁ and a path h. The bead walks h, runs δ at x₁, walks back: h δ h̄ is a loop at x₀.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Gyroid steps onto the pad, runs the gold petal along its arrows and steps back on; the pad pulses.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: All three petals; summary card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Fix a basepoint, $x₀$. A loop leaves it and comes back: a path $f$ with $f(0) = f(1) = x₀$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Loops that slide into one another, with $x₀$ pinned the whole time, count as the same. Their classes make up $π₁(X, x₀)$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: To multiply two loops, run one and then the other — each twice as fast, so the trip still takes one unit of time.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: That product, $f · g$, is the group law. It respects sliding, so it works on classes.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Standing still is the identity. Running a loop backwards, $f̄$, is its inverse.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Out and straight back — and if I go out less and less far, the whole trip shrinks onto the pad.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Three loops: $(α β) γ$ or $α (β γ)$? Watch the two beads — same trail, different timing.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Re-timing a loop is a homotopy, so the brackets don’t matter. With that, $π₁(X, x₀)$ is a group.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A second beacon, $x₁$, and a path $h$ to it. Walk $h$, run a loop $f$ at $x₁$, walk back: that’s a loop at $x₀$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So $[f] ↦ [h f h̄]$ matches every loop at $x₁$ with one at $x₀$. It’s an isomorphism: nothing gained, nothing lost.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Your Lash closes loops now. Start on the amber pad, run a petal along its arrows, and step back on.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Out… round… and home. And against the arrows, it’s the inverse.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: That’s the fundamental group at one point. Go and try it on the Bastion’s beacons.

videos.title: The Winding Number
videos.plays: Replay from Level 3 · ? How it works
videos.synopsis: The helix cover ℝ → S¹: path lifting, homotopy lifting, winding numbers in ℤ, and the in-game Cord and Tide Glass.

scenes.title: The covering
scenes.description: The helix over the ring road; a bead climbs the helix while its shadow runs round the circle, joined by a pink drop line (p). A pink column marks the lifts of one point, one per floor.

scenes.title: Lifting a loop
scenes.description: A loop of one lap lifts from floor 0 to +1; a loop of two laps lifts to +2.

scenes.title: Homotopy lifting
scenes.description: The one-lap loop deforms (teal on the ring); its lift sways, the end stays on the white bead at +1.

scenes.title: Laps add
scenes.description: Two laps up, then one back: the lift climbs to +2 and comes down to +1.

scenes.title: Winders
scenes.description: A Winder holding +2; two clockwise laps strip its coils.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Gyroid runs one lap with the Winding Cord and steps onto the beacon to bank it.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The circle has a cover: the helix. Over every point of the circle there’s a whole column of points — one on every floor.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Drop the helix straight down and it wraps onto the circle, once per floor. That map, $p : ℝ → S¹$, is the covering.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Run a loop on the circle and its lift climbs the helix, starting on floor $0$. One lap counter-clockwise ends on floor $+1$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Two laps — floor $+2$. The floor where the lift ends is the loop’s winding number.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now deform the loop. Its lift sways too, but the end can only sit on a floor, and it can’t hop from one floor to the next.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So loops that slide into each other end on the same floor: the winding number can’t change.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Run $+2$, then $−1$: the lift climbs two floors and comes down one. Winding numbers add.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So loops on the circle are just the integers: $π₁(S¹) ≅ ℤ$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Winders hold stolen turns, and the Lash slides off them. This one holds $+2$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Two clockwise laps: $2 + (−1) + (−1) = 0$. The coils fall away — now one lash will do.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Winding Cord (4): run the ring with the arrows for $+1$, against them for $−1$. Then step onto the beacon to bank the lap.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Tide Glass (3) deforms a banked loop. And the Lash (1) is for Winders, once they’re unwound.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Every loop on the circle comes down to one whole number. Go and read the floors.

videos.title: No Way Out
videos.plays: Lesson · World 1 · Level 4
videos.synopsis: Rim winding vs disk; no retraction; still points; roots; antipodes.

scenes.title: The rim loop
scenes.description: A bead walks the rim of the basin once; the pink arrow over it (its direction from the centre) turns once.

scenes.title: The Retractor
scenes.description: The rim loop shrinks to the centre; its image pushed back onto the rim (pink, dashed) stays a full lap until the loop is a point — the engine tears.

scenes.title: The still point
scenes.description: The swirl field of a map h; the bead walks the rim, the arrow turns once; the still tile pulses.

scenes.title: The roots
scenes.description: The field of z³ − a³; one lap turns the arrow three times; three whirlpools pulse.

scenes.title: The antipodes
scenes.description: The sphere of weather stations; the opposite pair with equal readings pulses.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Gyroid walks the rim road once round.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Walk the rim of a disk once and watch an arrow pointing out from the centre: it turns once. The rim loop winds once.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Inside the disk, though, that loop shrinks to a point — the disk has nothing to wind round.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Null’s Retractor claims to push the whole disk onto its rim. Then it would have to push every shrinking loop back out to the rim…

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: …and each of those winds once — until the last loop is a single point, which winds zero. A winding number can’t jump. So it tears: there’s no retraction $D² → S¹$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now a map $h$ of the disk to itself. At each spot an arrow points from $x$ toward $h(x)$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The arrow turns once round the rim. With no zero arrow, shrinking the rim would take one to zero. So some point stays put: $h(x) = x$. That’s Brouwer’s theorem.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Same trick for polynomials. Here the arrows follow $z³ − a³$. One lap of the rim — and the arrow turns three times.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So the arrows must vanish inside. Three whirlpools — three roots!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: And on a sphere: give every point two readings. Some point and its opposite always read the same — the Borsuk–Ulam theorem.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Winding Cord (4): walk each rim road once round and count the pink arrow over your head.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Tide Glass for the Retractor’s loop, then click what the count promises.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So if the count round the rim isn’t zero, something inside has to give.

videos.title: Push It Forward
videos.plays: Replay from Level 5 · ? How it works
videos.synopsis: Induced homomorphisms on S¹, retractions and injectivity, π₁(T²) ≅ ℤ², grid lift, and in-game Cord / projector / Sling.

scenes.title: Maps push loops forward
scenes.description: Source and target circles; z ↦ z² carries one lap of the source to two laps of the target, beads in step.

scenes.title: A retraction
scenes.description: An annulus round a pool: two laps of the inner road are pushed out onto the rim and stay two laps.

scenes.title: The torus
scenes.description: A square plaza with opposite gates glued; a bead goes a then b, then b then a; the lift on the grid beside reaches (1, 1) both times.

scenes.title: Products
scenes.description: Two factor circles: 2 laps and 3 laps make the loop (2, 3).

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Gyroid runs the source circle and stands at the projector.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card over the plaza.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A map between spaces carries every loop along with it. This one, $z ↦ z²$, wraps one circle twice round another.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: One lap on the source — two laps on the target. So on $π₁$ it’s “times two”.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A ring with a hole in the middle can be pushed straight out onto its rim. That push is a retraction.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Two laps round the pool land as two laps on the rim. So rim loops that differ can’t slide together inside — or pushing out would slide them together on the rim.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A torus, laid flat: a square whose opposite gates are glued. Leave by the east gate and come back in at the west — that’s the loop $a$. North and south: the loop $b$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The grid beside it is the plane that covers the torus. Each trip through a gate moves the lift one square.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: $a$ then $b$, or $b$ then $a$ — the same square, $(1, 1)$. So $ab = ba$, and $π₁(T²) ≅ ℤ × ℤ$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: And in general $π₁(X × Y) ≅ π₁(X) × π₁(Y)$: a loop on $S¹ × S¹$ is its two shadows — here, $2$ laps and $3$ laps.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Winding Cord (4): run the gold source circle once, then click the projector to push the loop forward.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: And if spawn are jamming it, Lash them first.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So a map pushes loops forward, and on a torus a loop is just a pair of whole numbers.

videos.title: Free Words
videos.plays: Replay in World 1 · Level 6
videos.synopsis: Laps print letters; adjacent inverses cancel; ab ≠ ba; demo laps and the Clasp.

scenes.title: A loop is a word
scenes.description: A bead runs the orange petal then the blue; the tape on the card reads a b.

scenes.title: Cancelling
scenes.description: a then a⁻¹ cancels to an empty tape; a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹ runs fast and nothing cancels.

scenes.title: Order matters
scenes.description: Two beads at once: white runs a then b, teal runs b then a; two tapes, two different words.

scenes.title: Undoing a word
scenes.description: The tape a b a⁻¹ is cancelled lap by lap by a, b⁻¹, a⁻¹.

scenes.title: The patrol
scenes.description: The ribbon patrol marches a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹; its letters are struck from the end and it unravels.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Gyroid runs the orange petal once.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Two loops meet at this beacon — a figure-eight. Every loop on it can be written as a word in $a$ and $b$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Run the orange petal: that’s $a$. Then the blue one: $b$. The tape reads $a b$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Run $a$, then run it backwards — $a⁻¹$. A letter right beside its own inverse cancels: the tape is empty again.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: $a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹$ — and nothing cancels. No letter sits beside its own inverse.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now $a b$ and $b a$, side by side. Two different reduced words — two different loops.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Different reduced words are always different loops here, so $ab ≠ ba$ in the free group $F₂$. On the torus they were equal; here they’re not.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: To undo a word, run its letters in reverse order, each one backwards. The tape $a b a⁻¹$ is undone by $a$, $b⁻¹$, $a⁻¹$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Each lap lands at the end and cancels the last letter — down to nothing.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The Commutator’s patrol marches $a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹$. It won’t cancel, so unravel it from the end: strike its last letter first.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: $b⁻¹$, $a⁻¹$, $b$, $a$ — gone.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Leave the beacon, run a petal all the way round, and come back. Along the arrows it’s the letter; against them, its inverse.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Go and spell some words.

videos.title: Glue and Van Kampen
videos.plays: Replay from Glue Job — ? How it works

scenes.title: A disk makes a relation
scenes.description: A loop a at a point; a disk fills it; a bead runs the loop as it slides across the disk to the point.

scenes.title: The torus
scenes.description: A square with edges a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹ rolls up into the torus.

scenes.title: The projective plane
scenes.description: A disk on a a: the projective plane, shown crossing itself.

scenes.title: Van Kampen
scenes.description: Two overlapping pieces, orange and blue; the loop round the overlap glows pink.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Gyroid forges the point, walks an edge, walks the word, presses the disk.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: The torus again; summary card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Glue a disk along a loop $a$, and the loop can slide across the disk down to a point.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So in the new space, $a$ is trivial. Gluing a disk adds a relation: $a = 1$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Two loops, $a$ and $b$, and a disk glued along $a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹$. The square rolls up — into the torus.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So $a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹ = 1$, which means $a b = b a$. That’s the torus’s $ℤ × ℤ$ again!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now one loop, and a disk glued along $a a$ — twice round. That makes the projective plane.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: There $a² = 1$: going round twice slides away, but once doesn’t. The group is $ℤ₂$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Van Kampen’s theorem says how groups glue. Split a space into two overlapping pieces, $U$ and $V$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Take all the words from both pieces — then, for each loop in the overlap, say that its name in $U$ equals its name in $V$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Cell Hammer (2): click the furnace to forge the point, then walk out round a track and back for an edge.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Then walk the word the disk should go along, and press the furnace. The Clasp (5) is for the overlap deck.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Each disk you glue adds one relation. Go and press some.

videos.title: Sheet Music
videos.plays: After the 1-9 intro; replayable from “How it works”
videos.synopsis: Connected covers ↔ subgroups; build a two-sheet order; conjugate by moving the start; walk the universal tree and the plane over a torus; then Clasp and Compass controls.

scenes.title: A cover built to order
scenes.description: Two sheets: a swaps them, b fixes both. The lift of a a closes; the lift of b closes.

scenes.title: Moving the start
scenes.description: A three-sheeted cover; from sheet 1 a opens, from sheet 3 a closes. The start sheet is ringed in pink.

scenes.title: The universal cover
scenes.description: The Cayley tree grows; the lift of a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹ walks to a new vertex.

scenes.title: The plane over the torus
scenes.description: A grid; a b lifts to (1, 1), a a⁻¹ b b⁻¹ back to (0, 0).

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Gyroid at the deck; the steps card.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: The tree again; summary card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Tell the Stacks which loops should close, and they’ll build a cover for it. Here: $a²$ and $b$ close, $a$ doesn’t — two sheets.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Twice round $a$ and my lift is home; $b$ never leaves the sheet. The loops that close make a subgroup.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now three sheets. From sheet 1, $b$ closes and $a$ doesn’t.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Start on sheet 3 instead, and it’s the other way round. Same cover, different start: the subgroups are conjugate.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: And if no loop should close but standing still? Then the cover is a tree: every reduced word ends at its own dot.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: $a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹$ just walks off to somewhere new. That’s the universal cover.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Over a torus, the universal cover is a plane. $a$ is one step east, $b$ one step north: $a b$ lands on $(1, 1)$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: And $a a⁻¹ b b⁻¹$ comes straight back to $(0, 0)$ — it closes.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The Clasp (5) re-glues sheets at a port. Lash the Stack sentinel (1) to move the start.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: And the Sheet Compass (6) works the tree’s branch tips and the torus pedestals.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Every connected cover is really a choice of which loops close. Go and choose some.

videos.title: Deck Shifts
videos.plays: Replay in World 1 · Level 10
videos.synopsis: Deck transformations, normal covers, and the antipodal sphere over RP².

scenes.title: A deck transformation
scenes.description: The cover a = b = (1 2 3) turns a third of the way round and lands on itself; white rings mark where the sheets were.

scenes.title: Not normal
scenes.description: The cover a = (1 2), b = (2 3) turns a third and its loops land in the wrong places; it turns back.

scenes.title: Covers from symmetry
scenes.description: The circle’s double cover: a half-turn swaps the two sheets.

scenes.title: The sphere over ℝP²
scenes.description: The sphere hall with opposite golden doors; a bead walks half the rim, door to door.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Gyroid beside the turning cover.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: The sphere hall; summary card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A deck transformation shuffles a cover’s sheets so that the whole cover lands on itself — every edge onto an edge with the same letter.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Turn this one a third of the way round, and it fits exactly. Any sheet can go to any other.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: When deck transformations can reach every sheet, the cover is normal, like that one. The next one isn’t.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Turned, its loops land in the wrong places. A deck transformation carries loops to loops, so only “do nothing” works.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Symmetry makes covers too. Turn a circle half way round: no point stays put.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Divide that out and you get a circle again, covered twice — $z ↦ z²$!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Same with a sphere and its opposite points: glue each point to its opposite, and you get the projective plane, $ℝP²$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Half the rim runs from a door to the opposite door. Down below, those doors are one point — so it’s a loop whose lift doesn’t close. $π₁(ℝP²) ≅ ℤ₂$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the halls, click the wheel with the Sheet Compass (6) to turn a cover.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Lash the Deck guards once they stack, and walk the sphere’s rim from door to door.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Turn the covers, then walk the sphere. Null’s trail runs out through the north gate.

videos.title: Higher Homotopy Groups
videos.plays: World 4 · Level 1 lesson
videos.synopsis: Higher homotopy groups: maps of cubes with their boundary at the base point, added side by side; abelian for n ≥ 2 because there is room to slide past.

scenes.title: πₙ(X, x₀)
scenes.description: A square’s four edges are pinned to the beacon.

scenes.title: Adding
scenes.description: f goes in the left half, g in the right: f + g.

scenes.title: Room to pass
scenes.description: f and g shrink, slide past each other, and regrow as g + f.

scenes.title: One dimension
scenes.description: On an interval f and g shrink, but can’t pass.

scenes.title: Higher groups
scenes.description: The swapped square again.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Tide Glass.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A loop sends both ends of an interval to the base point. Now take a square, and send its whole edge to $x₀$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Crush the edge to a point and the square becomes a sphere: a map $S² → X$. These, up to sliding, form $π₂(X, x₀)$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: To add $f$ and $g$, squeeze $f$ into the left half and $g$ into the right, like running one loop and then the other. Flip $f$ to get $−f$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So it’s joining loops, with more room.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now swap them. Shrink both into small boxes, slide one up and one down, move them past each other, and grow them back.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Outside the boxes everything stays on $x₀$, so the edge stays pinned at every step. $f + g ≃ g + f$: $πₙ$ is abelian for $n ≥ 2$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Try it on an interval, which is loops. Shrink them… and there’s no sideways to slide into.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So $π₁$ can fail to be abelian. On the figure-eight, $ab$ and $ba$ are different loops.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: From dimension two up, order never matters. The Commutator’s word $aba⁻¹b⁻¹$ is just zero here.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Wherever he went, he wouldn’t like it up here.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the Hall the Tide Glass (3) pins edges, places cubes, and steps through each slide.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Spheres mapped in and added side by side: the higher homotopy groups.

videos.title: Cellular Approximation
videos.plays: World 4 · Level 2 lesson
videos.synopsis: Cellular approximation: every map between CW complexes is homotopic to a cellular one, skeleton by skeleton; so πₖ(Sⁿ) = 0 for k < n.

scenes.title: Skeleta
scenes.description: A CW grid with a wiggly path.

scenes.title: Cellular maps
scenes.description: The path’s pieces snap onto grid lines.

scenes.title: Slip off
scenes.description: A loop in S²’s 2-cell is punctured and pushed out to e⁰.

scenes.title: Too small
scenes.description: A board of πₖ(Sⁿ): those with k < n marked 0.

scenes.title: The proof
scenes.description: Endpoints snap to 0-cells first, then the pieces to 1-cells.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Cell-Smith.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A CW complex: dots are 0-cells, lines 1-cells, squares 2-cells. Dots and lines make the 1-skeleton.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A map can wander anywhere. This path cuts straight across the squares.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Cellular approximation slides it, ends held still, into the 1-skeleton. Any map of CW complexes can be made cellular.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Snapped to the grid. Theorem 4.8.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now $S²$ as one 0-cell and one 2-cell: a disk with its whole rim glued to a point. A loop runs around inside the disk.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A loop can’t cover the disk, so it misses a point. Puncture there, push out to the rim, a single point: $π₁(S²) = 0$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The same works whenever $k < n$: a $k$-sphere can be slid off a point of an $n$-cell.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So $πₖ(Sⁿ) = 0$ for $k < n$. For $k ≥ n$ the theorem says nothing, and $π₃(S²)$ isn’t $0$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The proof climbs the skeleta: first the 0-cells land on dots, then the 1-cells on lines, and so on up.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Dots first, then lines. Never undo what’s already tidy.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the Gallery the Cell Hammer (2) snaps paths, punctures cells, and marks groups.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Every map can be snapped to the grid: cellular approximation.

videos.title: Whitehead's Theorem
videos.plays: World 4 · Level 3 lesson
videos.synopsis: A weak homotopy equivalence induces isomorphisms on all homotopy groups; between CW complexes it is a homotopy equivalence (Whitehead). Without a map, matching groups prove nothing.

scenes.title: Weak equivalence
scenes.description: Two rooms of homotopy meters.

scenes.title: Whitehead
scenes.description: S¹ ↪ ℝ² − 0: every courier green.

scenes.title: A weak spot
scenes.description: S² → point: the π₂ courier fails.

scenes.title: No map
scenes.description: ℝP² and S² × ℝP∞: the same meters, no route.

scenes.title: The certificate
scenes.description: Four pairs sorted.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Reading Wand.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A map $f: X → Y$ carries sphere-maps across, giving $f_*$ on each $πₙ$. All isomorphisms: a weak homotopy equivalence.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Each runner carries one $πₙ$ across. Green means $f_*$ is an isomorphism there.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The circle in the punctured plane: all green. Whitehead: for connected CW complexes, that makes it a homotopy equivalence.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: And the punctured plane really does shrink onto the circle.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $S²$ crushed to a point: $π₁$ is fine, but $π₂ = ℤ$ goes to $0$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: One red runner is enough. It’s not a weak equivalence, and $S²$ isn’t contractible.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $ℝP²$ and $S² × ℝP∞$ have the same homotopy groups in every degree.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: But their $H₂$ differ, so no map can induce those isomorphisms.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So the certificate is a map with every runner green. Matching numbers aren’t enough.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Two pairs certified, two not.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: At the Weak Spot the Reading Wand (0) sends runners and marks pairs.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A map that matches every group: Whitehead’s theorem.

videos.title: Freudenthal Suspension
videos.plays: World 4 · Level 4 lesson
videos.synopsis: Suspension lifts maps of spheres a dimension; Freudenthal makes it an isomorphism in the stable range, giving πₙ(Sⁿ) ≅ ℤ and stable stems such as πₙ₊₁(Sⁿ) = ℤ₂.

scenes.title: Suspension
scenes.description: A degree is dialled and the map is slung up from π₁(S¹) to π₂(S²).

scenes.title: Degree survives
scenes.description: A degree-2 map climbs to π₃(S³).

scenes.title: Freudenthal
scenes.description: A board of suspension maps; the isomorphisms are marked.

scenes.title: Stable range
scenes.description: The board, five tiles marked.

scenes.title: Stem 1
scenes.description: η climbs from π₃(S²) = ℤ to ℤ₂, ℤ₂, ℤ₂.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Sling and Dial.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Suspension cones a sphere up to one pole and down to another. $f: Sⁱ → Sⁿ$ becomes $Σf: Sⁱ⁺¹ → Sⁿ⁺¹$, $f$ on every latitude.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So suspension gives a homomorphism $πᵢ(Sⁿ) → πᵢ₊₁(Sⁿ⁺¹)$. The Sling does it.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A degree-$2$ map on $S¹$ suspends to degree $2$ on $S²$, then on $S³$. The degree survives every lift.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So every $πₙ(Sⁿ)$ is $ℤ$, read off by degree!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Freudenthal’s theorem: $πᵢ(Sⁿ) → πᵢ₊₁(Sⁿ⁺¹)$ is an isomorphism when $i < 2n − 1$, when the source sphere isn’t too big…

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: …and onto when $i = 2n − 1$. That’s Theorem 4.23.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Fix the stem $k = i − n$, the gap between the spheres. Once $n > k + 1$, every suspension is an isomorphism.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The groups stop changing. Those are the stable homotopy groups of spheres.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Stem 1: the Hopf map $η$ in $π₃(S²) = ℤ$ suspends onto $π₄(S³) = ℤ₂$. That step is only onto. After it, $ℤ₂$ for good.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Stable ground. The first stem settles at $ℤ₂$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: At the Landing the Sling (4) suspends, and the Degree Dial (8) sets degrees and marks tiles.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Lift a map high enough and nothing changes: Freudenthal suspension.
