videos.synopsis: Eilenberg–MacLane spaces K(G, n) have a single non-zero homotopy group; S¹, the torus and ℝP∞ are K(G, 1)s; killing the higher groups of S² cell by cell builds K(ℤ, 2) = ℂP∞.

scenes.title: K(G, n)
scenes.description: Five spaces on pedestals.

scenes.title: K(G, 1)s
scenes.description: The circle, the torus and ℝP∞ light as K(G, 1)s.

scenes.title: Not K(G, 1)s
scenes.description: S² and ℝP² are marked not.

scenes.title: Kill above
scenes.description: S²’s higher homotopy groups are killed one at a time.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Cell-Smith.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Some spaces have just one non-zero homotopy group. If $πₙ = G$ and every other one is $0$, the space is a $K(G, n)$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: One kind of hole, in one dimension. They’re the bricks of homotopy theory, and of cohomology too, as you’ll see.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $S¹$ is a $K(ℤ, 1)$, the torus a $K(ℤ², 1)$, $ℝP∞$ a $K(ℤ₂, 1)$. Their universal covers, $ℝ$, $ℝ²$ and $S∞$, all shrink to a point.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: And a covering doesn’t change $πₙ$ for $n ≥ 2$. So nothing’s left above $π₁$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $S²$ isn’t one: $π₂(S²) = ℤ$, and there’s more above.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Nor is $ℝP²$. Its universal cover is $S²$, so $π₂(ℝP²) = ℤ$ as well.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: To build $K(ℤ, 2)$, start from $S²$. To kill $π₃$, glue on a $4$-cell along a map $S³ → S²$ that generates it.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: New $(k+1)$-cells kill $πₖ$ and can’t touch the groups below. The ones above can change.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So kill them in order, $π₃$, $π₄$, $π₅$, forever. What’s left is $K(ℤ, 2)$, which Hatcher shows is $ℂP∞$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: One group per floor, everything else filled in. That’s his Spire.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: At One Group: the Cell Hammer (2) marks spaces and attaches the cells that kill each group.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: One group, one dimension: Eilenberg–MacLane spaces.

videos.title: The Hurewicz Map
videos.plays: World 4 · Level 6 lesson
videos.synopsis: The Hurewicz map from homotopy to homology is an isomorphism in the first non-zero degree of an (n−1)-connected space (n ≥ 2), abelianization in degree 1, and promises nothing above.

scenes.title: The Hurewicz map
scenes.description: Homotopy meters on the left, homology on the right.

scenes.title: Two meters
scenes.description: S²’s meters read row by row.

scenes.title: Hurewicz
scenes.description: S³, S² ∨ S², ℂP²: the first non-zero row of each is found.

scenes.title: Degree one
scenes.description: The figure-eight’s degree-1 bridge: abelianization.

scenes.title: Beyond the first
scenes.description: S²’s bridges: 1 and 2 hold, 3 fails.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Degree Dial.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Map a sphere in, $f: Sⁿ → X$, and count how it covers $X$, with signs: a class in $Hₙ(X)$. That’s the Hurewicz map, $h$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A bridge from one kind of count to the other. The question is where it holds.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $S²$: $π₁ = H₁ = 0$, $π₂ = H₂ = ℤ$. Then $π₃(S²) = ℤ$, while $H₃(S²) = 0$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: They agree at the first row where anything happens.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Say every sphere of dimension below $n$ shrinks in $X$, and $n ≥ 2$. Hurewicz: homology below $n$ is zero too, and $πₙ ≅ Hₙ$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $S³$ first lights up in degree $3$; $S² ∨ S²$ and $ℂP²$ in degree $2$. The bridge holds at each.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In degree $1$ the bridge is onto, and it loses exactly the commutators: $aba⁻¹b⁻¹$ counts as $a + b − a − b = 0$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: For the figure-eight, the free group on $a$ and $b$ goes onto $ℤ²$. $H₁$ is $π₁$ made abelian.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Above the first degree there’s no promise at all. $S²$’s third bridge fails.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: $π₃(S²) = ℤ$, $H₃(S²) = 0$. Homology can’t even see it.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the Hall: the Degree Dial (8) reads meters and tests bridges.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Where homotopy first shows up, homology agrees: the Hurewicz theorem.

videos.title: The Hopf Fibration
videos.plays: World 4 · Level 7 lesson
videos.synopsis: The Hopf fibration S¹ → S³ → S²: a circle over each point, any two linked once; its long exact sequence gives π₃(S²) ≅ ℤ, so the Hopf map is essential.

scenes.title: The Hopf map
scenes.description: A little S² beside the space of S³, drawn stereographically.

scenes.title: Fibres
scenes.description: Four points of S² are touched; four circles light.

scenes.title: Linked
scenes.description: Two fibres pass through each other once.

scenes.title: Exact sequence
scenes.description: The row π₃(S¹) → π₃(S³) → π₃(S²) → π₂(S¹).

scenes.title: π₃(S²)
scenes.description: The unknown lock tries 0, then ℤ.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Compass and Dial.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Pairs $(z₁, z₂)$ of complex numbers with $|z₁|² + |z₂|² = 1$ make $S³$. The Hopf map keeps only the ratio $z₁ : z₂$, a point of $S²$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Multiply both by the same unit complex number and the ratio stays put. So over each point of $S²$ lies a whole circle.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: We draw $S³$ by stereographic projection. Touch a point of $S²$ and its circle lights. Every point of $S³$ is on exactly one.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: A whole three-sphere, made of circles.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Look at any two fibres: they link, once, every time.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Linked circles don’t come apart without cutting. That’s the picture that says the map isn’t trivial. The proof comes next.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A fibre bundle: every fibre the same, and locally a product. Theorem 4.41 gives it a long exact row of homotopy groups.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Exact: what arrives at each group is just what the next map kills. Here $π₃(S¹) = π₂(S¹) = 0$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So $π₃(S²)$ sits between two zeros, next to $π₃(S³) = ℤ$. It must be $ℤ$, generated by the Hopf map.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: A map from a bigger sphere that won’t squash flat.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: At the Ring: the Sheet Compass (6) lights fibres; the Degree Dial (8) tries groups.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Circles over a sphere, linked once: the Hopf fibration.

videos.title: Stable Homotopy
videos.plays: World 4 · Level 8 lesson
videos.synopsis: Each stem πₙ₊ₖ(Sⁿ) settles from n = k + 2 on; its stable value is πₖˢ — ℤ, ℤ₂, ℤ₂, ℤ₂₄ for the first four stems.

scenes.title: The table
scenes.description: The wall of πₙ₊ₖ(Sⁿ), stems in rows.

scenes.title: Settling
scenes.description: Each stem’s first stable tile lights.

scenes.title: Stem 3
scenes.description: Stem 3 changes three times, then settles at ℤ₂₄.

scenes.title: Stable groups
scenes.description: The stable values are set: ℤ, ℤ₂, ℤ₂, ℤ₂₄.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Sling.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Hatcher opens Chapter 4 with a table of $πᵢ(Sⁿ)$. Read it by stems: fix $k$ and watch $πₙ₊ₖ(Sⁿ)$ as $n$ grows.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Each row of our wall is one stem. One step right is one suspension.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Freudenthal says suspension is an isomorphism when $n + k < 2n − 1$, that is, $n ≥ k + 2$. From there on a stem never changes.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So each stem settles one step later than the one above it.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Stem 3 shows why you need the range: $ℤ₂$, $ℤ₁₂$, $ℤ × ℤ₁₂$…

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: …and then $ℤ₂₄$, for good.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The settled value is the stable homotopy group $πₖˢ$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Stem 0: $ℤ$, the degree. Stem 1: $ℤ₂$, the Hopf map slung up. Stem 2: $ℤ₂$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Stem 3: $ℤ₂₄$. Further out they get wild. Nobody knows them all.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Nothing moving under my feet. I’ll take it while it lasts.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: On Stable Ground: the Suspension Sling (4) marks where stems settle and sets their values.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Up here the numbers settle: the stable homotopy groups.

videos.title: Cohomology as Maps
videos.plays: World 4 · Level 9 lesson
videos.synopsis: Cohomology is represented: Hⁿ(X; G) ≅ [X, K(G, n)] by f ↦ f*(ι). With K(ℤ, 1) = S¹, circle maps are classified by degree, and maps T² → S¹ by two windings — H¹(T²) = ℤ².

scenes.title: Eilenberg–MacLane
scenes.description: A circle map on the pedestal; its reading floats above.

scenes.title: Pull back
scenes.description: The lever steps the degree; the reading follows.

scenes.title: The circle
scenes.description: Degree 3 gives 3α; degree −2 gives −2α.

scenes.title: The torus
scenes.description: Two levers wind a torus map round a and b, reaching 2α − β.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Cup Caster.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A $K(G, n)$ has a single homotopy group, $πₙ = G$, and nothing else. The circle is a $K(ℤ, 1)$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Its one basic class is $ι ∈ Hⁿ(K(G, n); G)$. On the circle, $ι$ counts turns.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Map $X$ in with $f$ and read $ι$ along it: that’s the class $f*(ι)$ on $X$. Homotopic maps give the same class.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So a map into $K(G, n)$ is a way to read a class off $X$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Theorem 4.57: for a CW complex $X$, every class comes from a map, and from only one up to homotopy.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A circle map of degree $d$ turns each lap into $d$ laps, so $ι$ pulls back to $dα$. Degree $3$: $3α$. Degree $−2$: $−2α$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now map the torus to the circle. Round each loop of the torus, the image winds a whole number of times.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Twice round $a$ gives $2α$…

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: …and once backwards round $b$ adds $−β$: the class $2α − β$. So $[T², S¹] = H¹(T²) = ℤ²$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Two levers, two integers. Every setting is a class.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the Classing Room the Cup Caster (9) turns each lever. Make the maps each station asks for.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A class in $Hⁿ(X; G)$ is a map $X → K(G, n)$, up to homotopy.

videos.title: Fibrations and Lifts
videos.plays: World 4 · Level 10 lesson
videos.synopsis: A fibration lifts homotopies once a start is chosen. Any map f: A → B becomes a fibration E_f → B with E_f ≃ A; for a point in B this is the path fibration ΩB → PB → B, and PB contractible gives πₙ(ΩB) ≅ πₙ₊₁(B).

scenes.title: Lifting
scenes.description: A helix over a circle; a base loop lifts from sheet 1 to sheet 3.

scenes.title: The start decides
scenes.description: A backwards loop lifts from sheet 2 to sheet 1.

scenes.title: Make it a fibration
scenes.description: Two points over the ends of a bar; tethers make every fibre nonempty.

scenes.title: The loop space
scenes.description: The groups of ΩS² fill in from those of S², shifted by one.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Sheet Compass.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $p: E → B$ is a fibration if homotopies lift: move something in $B$, say where it starts in $E$, and the motion lifts.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The helix over the circle is one. Each turn climbs a sheet: wind twice from sheet $1$ and you end on sheet $3$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: For a covering the lift is unique once you choose the start. Wind backwards once from sheet $2$ and you come down to sheet $1$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: A loop down here. Up there it doesn’t even close.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Not every map is a fibration. Two points over the ends of a bar: over the middle there’s nothing to lift to.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Fix it with tethers: $E_f$ is pairs $(a, γ)$, $γ$ a path from $f(a)$. Every fibre fills, and $E_f$ still shrinks onto $A$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Tether just the base point and you get $PB$, paths from the base point. Its fibre is the loops: $ΩB$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $PB$ shrinks to a point, so the exact sequence gives $πₙ(ΩB) ≅ πₙ₊₁(B)$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: For $S²$: $π₁(ΩS²) = ℤ$, $π₂(ΩS²) = ℤ$, $π₃(ΩS²) = π₄(S²) = ℤ₂$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: The loops carry the sphere’s groups, one dimension down.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Here the Sheet Compass (6) picks start sheets, strings tethers and sets the loop-space groups.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A fibration: homotopies below lift, once you choose where they start.

videos.title: Postnikov Towers
videos.plays: World 4 · Level 11 lesson
videos.synopsis: A Postnikov tower builds X one homotopy group at a time: Xₙ has π₁ … πₙ of X, each step is a fibration with fibre K(πₙX, n), and k-invariants kₙ ∈ Hⁿ⁺²(Xₙ; πₙ₊₁X) say how the floors twist. S² and S³ × ℂP∞ have the same groups and different twists.

scenes.title: Postnikov floors
scenes.description: S²’s groups on three floors; the groups above each floor go out.

scenes.title: Fibres
scenes.description: Each step of the tower gets its Eilenberg–MacLane fibre.

scenes.title: k-invariants
scenes.description: The floors rise from the bottom, each the fibre of a k-invariant.

scenes.title: Same groups
scenes.description: Two towers with the same floors; one is twisted.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Cell-Smith and Cup Caster.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A Postnikov tower: each $Xₙ$ keeps $X$’s groups up to $πₙ$, and nothing above. For $S²$: $π₂ = ℤ$, $π₃ = ℤ$, $π₄ = ℤ₂$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Attach cells to kill everything above $n$. $X₂$ keeps only $π₂$; $X₃$ keeps $π₂$ and $π₃$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Each step $Xₙ → Xₙ₋₁$ is a fibration that adds one group, so its fibre is a $K(πₙX, n)$: here $K(ℤ, 2)$, $K(ℤ, 3)$, $K(ℤ₂, 4)$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So it’s Eilenberg–MacLane spaces all the way up.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: How is each floor set down? For $S²$, $Xₙ₊₁$ is the homotopy fibre of a map $kₙ: Xₙ → K(πₙ₊₁X, n + 2)$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: By Theorem 4.57 that map is a class, the k-invariant $kₙ ∈ Hⁿ⁺²(Xₙ; πₙ₊₁X)$: the twist.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: If every $kₙ$ is $0$, nothing is twisted, and $X$ is just the product of its $K(πₙX, n)$’s.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $S²$ and $S³ × ℂP∞$ share their groups. $S³ × ℂP∞$ has $k₂ = 0$: its $X₃$ is $K(ℤ, 2) × K(ℤ, 3)$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: That product has $H₃ = ℤ$. $S²$’s $X₃$ has $S²$’s homology up to degree $3$, so $H₃ = 0$. $S²$’s $k₂$ isn’t $0$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Same floors. One twisted, one not. Two different spaces.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The Twist: Cell Hammer (2) kills groups and raises floors; Cup Caster (9) names fibres and sets twists.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A Postnikov tower: one Eilenberg–MacLane floor per group, glued by the k-invariants.

videos.title: Obstruction Theory
videos.plays: World 4 · Level 12 lesson
videos.synopsis: To extend a map A → X over W, go cell by cell: an (n+1)-cell extends when its boundary is null in πₙ(X). The obstructions form a class ωₙ ∈ Hⁿ⁺¹(W, A; πₙX); the extension continues iff it is 0, and if all these groups vanish every map extends.

scenes.title: Cell by cell
scenes.description: Low cells fill; the 3-cell stays red.

scenes.title: The obstruction
scenes.description: Three 3-cells read their obstructions; the zero one fills.

scenes.title: Reroute
scenes.description: A twist on the shared cell clears one pair; the next pair can’t be cleared.

scenes.title: Guaranteed
scenes.description: The doors whose obstruction groups vanish open.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Cell-Smith and Cup Caster.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The extension problem. A map is known on $A$. Can you fill it in over all of $W$? Go one cell at a time.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: An $(n+1)$-cell fills when the map on its rim sphere $Sⁿ$ shrinks to a point. If $πₙ(X) = 0$, it always does: Lemma 4.7.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Into $S²$, a $3$-cell’s rim is a map $S² → S²$: a degree, in $π₂(S²) = ℤ$. Zero, and the cell fills. Not zero, and it’s blocked.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Two blocked, one through.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Change the map on a $2$-cell between two $3$-cells, and their numbers shift by $+k$ and $−k$. Here $1$ and $−1$ both clear.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: With $2$ and $0$ no twist works: the sum stays $2$. The obstruction is a class, $ωₙ ∈ Hⁿ⁺¹(W, A; πₙX)$. Extend iff $ωₙ = 0$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So if all the groups $Hⁿ⁺¹(W, A; πₙX)$ vanish, nothing can block you. That’s Corollary 4.73.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $(D², S¹)$ into $S²$: one $2$-cell, so the only group is $H²(D², S¹; π₁S²)$, and $π₁S² = 0$. It extends.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Into $S¹$, $π₂$ and up vanish, and $H²(D³, S²; ℤ) = 0$: that extends too. $(D³, S²)$ into $S²$ meets $H³ = ℤ$: no guarantee.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Last floor. Every wall on it was a reading.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Obstruction Course: Cell Hammer (2) extends and opens doors; Cup Caster (9) reads obstructions and twists cells.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: What blocks an extension, cell by cell, is a cohomology class.

videos.title: Readings and Coboundaries
videos.plays: World 3 · Level 1 lesson
videos.synopsis: Cochains read chains; δφ = φ∂; cocycles balance on every simplex; coboundaries come from point values; a cocycle that is not a coboundary sees a hole.

scenes.title: Cochains
scenes.description: A triangle with readings on its edges; it reads 3.

scenes.title: Cocycles
scenes.description: One edge changes until the triangle reads 0.

scenes.title: Balancing the fan
scenes.description: The fan’s spokes are set one by one until every triangle balances.

scenes.title: Coboundaries
scenes.description: Point values are set until every edge reads its target.

scenes.title: Cohomology
scenes.description: A reading balanced on the filled tile, non-zero round the missing one.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Reading Wand.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A 1-cochain $φ$ puts a number on every edge. Read it on a path by adding the numbers along it. Hatcher writes $Cⁿ(X; G) = $ Hom$(Cₙ(X), G)$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Its coboundary gives each triangle the sum of $φ$ round its edges: $δφ(σ) = φ(∂σ)$. Here that’s $2 − 0 + 1 = 3$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Change an edge until the triangle reads $0$, and $φ$ is a cocycle: $δφ = 0$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: And since $δφ = φ∂$, $δδ = φ∂∂ = 0$. For free!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: On the fan, the rim is fixed. Set one spoke, and each triangle pins down the next.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Shift every spoke by the same amount and it still balances. That shift is $δ$ of a reading at the centre point.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A 0-cochain puts a number on each point, like a height. Its coboundary gives each edge head minus tail: $δf[v w] = f(w) − f(v)$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: An edge reading that comes from heights like this is a coboundary.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Coboundaries read $0$ round every loop. So a cocycle that reads non-zero round the missing tile can’t be one.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Cocycles modulo coboundaries: $H¹$ = Ker δ / Im δ. It sees the hole too!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the Pools: the Reading Wand (0) changes the value on an edge or a point.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Numbers on cells, kept when they balance, ignored when they’re just differences: cohomology.

videos.title: Torsion Climbs
videos.plays: World 3 · Level 2 lesson
videos.synopsis: The universal coefficient theorem: free parts of homology stay in their degree, torsion shifts up one; with ℤ₂ coefficients a ℤ₂ appears in two degrees.

scenes.title: Universal coefficients
scenes.description: Two terraces: homology on the left, cohomology on the right.

scenes.title: All free
scenes.description: The torus’ four free summands each stay on their own floor.

scenes.title: Torsion climbs
scenes.description: ℝP²: ℤ stays, the ℤ₂ climbs a floor.

scenes.title: Change the soil
scenes.description: ℝP² with ℤ₂ coefficients: ℤ₂ on every floor.

scenes.title: Corollary 3.3
scenes.description: The Klein bottle: ℤ, ℤ, then ℤ₂ on top.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Reading Wand.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Cohomology is read off the same chains as homology, so it’s no surprise that one almost determines the other.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The universal coefficient theorem: $Hⁿ(X; G) ≅$ Hom$(Hₙ(X), G) ⊕$ Ext$(Hₙ₋₁(X), G)$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: For the torus every piece is free, and Hom$(ℤ, ℤ) = ℤ$: each one stays on its own floor.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So $H⁰ = ℤ$, $H¹ = ℤ²$, $H² = ℤ$ — the same as homology.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $ℝP²$ has $H₁ = ℤ₂$. Hom$(ℤ₂, ℤ) = 0$, so nothing stays on floor one…

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: …but Ext$(ℤ₂, ℤ) = ℤ₂$ appears one floor up. $H²(ℝP²; ℤ) = ℤ₂$, though $H₂(ℝP²) = 0$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Change the soil to $ℤ₂$. Now Hom$(ℤ₂, ℤ₂) = ℤ₂$ and Ext$(ℤ₂, ℤ₂) = ℤ₂$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary

videos.title: The Cup Product
videos.plays: World 3 · Level 3 lesson
videos.synopsis: The cup product multiplies cochains face by face; on the torus α ⌣ β reads 1 on the whole surface, β ⌣ α = −α ⌣ β, and α ⌣ α = 0.

scenes.title: The cup product
scenes.description: One triangle with readings φ and ψ on its edges.

scenes.title: One triangle
scenes.description: The caster takes φ’s front face, then ψ’s back face; the lantern reads 6.

scenes.title: The torus
scenes.description: α ⌣ β cast on both triangles; the torus lantern reads +1.

scenes.title: Order matters
scenes.description: β ⌣ α instead: the torus lantern reads −1.

scenes.title: On cohomology
scenes.description: α ⌣ α reads 0; α ⌣ β reads +1.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Two readings can be multiplied. For $φ ∈ Cᵏ$ and $ψ ∈ Cˡ$, the cup product $φ ⌣ ψ$ reads $(k+l)$-simplices.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $φ$ reads the simplex’s front face, $ψ$ its back face, and you multiply: $(φ ⌣ ψ)(σ) = φ(σ|[v₀…vₖ]) · ψ(σ|[vₖ…vₖ₊ₗ])$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: On one triangle: $φ$ on the front edge $[v₀v₁]$ reads $2$; $ψ$ on the back edge $[v₁v₂]$ reads $3$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So the lantern reads $6$ — and $[v₀v₂]$ never gets a say.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now the torus. $α$ reads $1$ on the $a$ edges, $β$ on the $b$ edges, both on the diagonal. Cast $α ⌣ β$ on each triangle…

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: …$1$ on the lower one, $0$ on the upper. Over the whole torus, $α ⌣ β$ reads $1$: it generates $H²(T)$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Swap them. $β ⌣ α$ reads $0$ and $1$ — and with the upper triangle’s orientation, the total is $−1$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: For two 1-classes, $β ⌣ α = −α ⌣ β$. So $α ⌣ α = −α ⌣ α$, which forces it to be $0$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: And since $δ(φ ⌣ ψ) = δφ ⌣ ψ ± φ ⌣ δψ$, cocycles cup to cocycles: ⌣ works on cohomology classes.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: $α ⌣ α$: dark. $α ⌣ β$: lit!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the Rows: the Cup Caster (9) casts on edges and triangles, and levers choose the readings.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Front face, back face: the cup product.

scenes.title: The torus
scenes.description: α ⌣ β lights the torus lantern.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The torus, and $S¹ ∨ S¹ ∨ S²$: two circles and a sphere, joined at one point.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Their cohomology groups match in every degree: $ℤ$, $ℤ²$, $ℤ$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: On the torus, the two 1-dimensional classes $α$ and $β$ cup to a generator of $H²$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: The top lantern blazes!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: On the bouquet, $α$ lives on one ring and $β$ on the other, and the sphere hangs from a single point.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Cup products are natural, so $α ⌣ β$ is pulled back from there — and it’s $0$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A homotopy equivalence would carry one cup product to the other. These don’t match, so the spaces aren’t equivalent.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Same groups, different products. The torus stays.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: On the Islands: the Cup Caster (9) reads meters and casts on triangles, rings and lanterns.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Cohomology is a ring — and the ring sees more than the groups.

videos.title: Products of Readings
videos.plays: World 3 · Level 5 lesson
videos.synopsis: Cross products of classes give classes on products, in the sum of the degrees; the Künneth formula says (with free cohomology or field coefficients) they make up all of H*(X × Y).

scenes.title: Cross products
scenes.description: A grid of beds: rows from X, columns from Y; bins by degree.

scenes.title: S¹ × S¹
scenes.description: Four beds go to bins 0, 1, 1, 2 — the torus.

scenes.title: S² × S²
scenes.description: Four beds go to bins 0, 2, 2, 4.

scenes.title: Over a field

scenes.title: Künneth
scenes.description: The X and Y levers become S¹ and S²; the bins read 1, 1, 1, 1.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Cup Caster.

scenes.title: Summary

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A class $a$ of degree $p$ on $X$ and a class $b$ of degree $q$ on $Y$ give a cross product $a × b$ on $X × Y$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Its degree is $p + q$. Rows are classes of $X$, columns classes of $Y$: every bed is one cross product.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $S¹ × S¹$: $1 × 1$ in degree $0$, two beds in degree $1$, and $α × α$ in degree $2$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Ranks $1, 2, 1$ — that’s the torus!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: And the cup product of the two degree-2 classes is the top class: $(γ × 1) ⌣ (1 × γ) = γ × γ$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Torsion complicates Künneth over $ℤ$, so use a field: $ℤ₂$. Then $ℝP² × ℝP²$ is just as easy.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Degree $2$: $a² × 1$, $a × a$, $1 × a²$ — three beds, so $H² = ℤ₂³$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The Künneth formula: $H*(X × Y) ≅ H*(X) ⊗ H*(Y)$, when the cohomology is free or the coefficients are a field.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So ranks multiply like polynomials: $S¹ × S²$ gives $1, 1, 1, 1$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the Parterre: the Cup Caster (9) moves a bed to its bin; levers choose $X$ and $Y$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Rows times columns: the cohomology of a product.

videos.title: Truncated Polynomials
videos.plays: World 3 · Level 6 lesson
videos.synopsis: The cohomology rings of projective spaces are truncated polynomial rings on one generator; the truncation rules out maps such as ℝP⁴ → ℝP² nonzero on H¹ with ℤ₂ coefficients.

scenes.title: Powers of one class
scenes.description: A fountain with α lit on its first tier.

scenes.title: ℝP³ over ℤ₂
scenes.description: α ⌣ α lights α².

scenes.title: ℝPⁿ
scenes.description: ℝP⁴: α², α³, α⁴ light every tier.

scenes.title: ℂPⁿ
scenes.description: ℂP³: α, α², α³ light the even tiers; α⁴ fizzles.

scenes.title: No such map
scenes.description: ℝP⁴ and ℝP² climbed together: α³ lights one and fizzles on the other.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Cup Caster.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In some spaces a single cohomology class makes all the others — just multiply it by itself.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Each fountain has a tier for every degree. Casting $α$ onto the top lit tier lights the next power.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $ℝP³$ with $ℤ₂$ coefficients: $α$ is in degree $1$, and $α ⌣ α = α²$ is not zero.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: On the torus $α²$ was zero — but mod 2, $−1 = 1$, so that argument fails.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $ℝP⁴$: $α$, $α²$, $α³$, $α⁴$ light every tier.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So $H*(ℝPⁿ; ℤ₂) = ℤ₂[α]/(αⁿ⁺¹)$: a polynomial ring, cut off at the dimension.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $ℂP³$ with $ℤ$ coefficients: now $α$ lives in degree $2$, so only the even tiers light.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: And $α⁴$ fizzles — it would need degree $8$. $H*(ℂPⁿ) = ℤ[α]/(αⁿ⁺¹)$: Theorem 3.12.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Suppose a map $f: ℝP⁴ → ℝP²$ had $f*(α) = α$. Then $f*(α³) = α³$… but $α³ = 0$ on $ℝP²$ and not on $ℝP⁴$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So no such map exists. That’s the idea behind Borsuk–Ulam!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the Garden: the Cup Caster (9) multiplies the top lit power by $α$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: One generator, all its powers: rings of projective spaces.

videos.title: Orientations
videos.plays: World 3 · Level 7 lesson
videos.synopsis: Local orientations, orientable manifolds, the orientable double cover, and the theorem that a closed connected manifold is orientable exactly when its top homology is ℤ.

scenes.title: Local orientation
scenes.description: An annulus of six patches, each with a compass.

scenes.title: Orientable
scenes.description: Two compasses flip; every compass agrees.

scenes.title: The Möbius band
scenes.description: A compass is carried round the twisted band and comes back flipped.

scenes.title: Double cover
scenes.description: A bead rides the two rings of the double cover, switching ring after one trip.

scenes.title: Theorem 3.26
scenes.description: Three bands surveyed: 0, 1, 2 half-twists.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Sheet Compass.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Near any point $x$ of an $n$-manifold, $Hₙ(M, M − x) ≅ ℤ$. Choosing a generator is a local orientation.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: On a surface that’s just a way round: counter-clockwise or clockwise. Our compasses.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: An orientation is a choice at every point that agrees with its neighbours. Flip the blue compasses on the annulus…

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: …and they all agree. The annulus is orientable.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The Möbius band has a half-twist. Carry a compass round, patch by patch…

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: …and it comes back pointing the other way. No consistent choice exists: non-orientable.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Put the two local orientations over each point and you get the orientable double cover, $M̃$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Over the Möbius band one lap switches sheets, so $M̃$ is one piece. Over an orientable $M$, two.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: For closed manifolds homology knows: $Hₙ(M; ℤ) ≅ ℤ$ exactly when $M$ is orientable. (Even twists cancel; odd ones don’t.)

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Theorem 3.26 — the torus has a fundamental class; the Klein bottle doesn’t.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: On the Cliffs: the Sheet Compass (6) flips and carries compasses, and rides the double cover.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Which way is up — and when the question has an answer.

videos.plays: World 3 · Level 8 lesson
videos.synopsis: Poincaré duality: on a closed R-orientable n-manifold, Hᵏ ≅ Hₙ₋ₖ; dual cells show why; over ℤ₂ it holds for every closed manifold.

scenes.description: The torus’ cohomology towers on one side of the seam, homology on the other.

scenes.title: Twin towers
scenes.description: Pairs light across the seam: H⁰–H₂, H¹–H₁, H²–H₀.

scenes.title: Dual cells
scenes.description: Each cell of the torus lights its dual cell in pink.

scenes.title: Broken mirror
scenes.description: ℝP²: over ℤ the pairs fail; over ℤ₂ they match.

scenes.title: Across the seam
scenes.description: The 3-torus: H₂ and H₃ rise to match H¹ and H⁰.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Sheet Compass.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: On a closed manifold with an orientation, cohomology and homology mirror each other across the dimension.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Poincaré duality: $Hᵏ(M) ≅ Hₙ₋ₖ(M)$, given by capping with the fundamental class $[M]$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The torus has $n = 2$: $H⁰$ pairs with $H₂$, $H¹$ with $H₁$, $H²$ with $H₀$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: $ℤ$, $ℤ²$, $ℤ$ on both sides — in reverse order!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Why? Draw the dual cells. Each $k$-cell meets exactly one dual $(n−k)$-cell.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The face becomes a point, each edge a crossing edge, the point a whole face. The chains run backwards.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $ℝP²$ has no orientation, so no $ℤ$ fundamental class — and over $ℤ$ the pairs don’t match.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: But every manifold is $ℤ₂$-orientable. Over $ℤ₂$, the mirror works.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The 3-torus: its cohomology is $ℤ$, $ℤ³$, $ℤ³$, $ℤ$. Duality says $H₂ ≅ H¹$ and $H₃ ≅ H⁰$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So $H₂ = ℤ³$ and $H₃ = ℤ$ — the fundamental class.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: At the Seam: the Sheet Compass (6) pairs towers, lights dual cells, and switches coefficients.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Two sides of one story: Poincaré duality.

videos.title: Perfect Pairings
videos.plays: World 3 · Level 9 lesson
videos.synopsis: The cup product pairing on a closed orientable manifold is nonsingular modulo torsion: every class has a partner. Hence α² generates H⁴(ℂP²), and S² ∨ S⁴ is not ℂP².

scenes.title: The cup pairing
scenes.description: The torus’ lanterns: classes on the left, partners on the right, the top lantern at the north.

scenes.title: The torus
scenes.description: α pairs with β, β with α.

scenes.title: S² × S²
scenes.description: γ × 1 pairs with 1 × γ.

scenes.title: ℂP²
scenes.description: α pairs with itself; the top lantern lights.

scenes.title: S² ∨ S⁴
scenes.description: α ⌣ α stays dark.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Cup Caster.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: On a closed orientable $n$-manifold, cup a class of degree $k$ with one of degree $n − k$ and read the result on $[M]$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Proposition 3.38: this pairing is nonsingular, modulo torsion. Every generator has a partner it cups with to $±1$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: On the torus, $α ⌣ α = 0$, so $α$ isn’t its own partner. But $α ⌣ β = 1$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: And $β$ partners $α$ — with a minus sign.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $S² × S²$: in the middle degree, $γ × 1$ and $1 × γ$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Each squares to $0$, but their product is the top class. Partners.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $ℂP²$ has only one middle class, $α$. It needs a partner — and the only candidate is $α$ itself.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So $α ⌣ α$ generates $H⁴(ℂP²)$. That’s how Hatcher finds the ring of $ℂPⁿ$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $S² ∨ S⁴$ has the same groups as $ℂP²$. But there $α ⌣ α = 0$: $α$ has no partner.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So it isn’t a closed orientable manifold, and it isn’t $ℂP²$!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: On the Pier: the Cup Caster (9) — a class on the left, a partner on the right.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Every lantern has a partner: the perfect pairing.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A simplex is a point, an edge, a triangle, a tetrahedron… with its corners numbered in order: $0$, $1$, $2$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Each arrow runs from the lower corner to the higher. It just says which end comes first.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A Δ-complex glues simplices face to face, but only in order: first corner onto first corner.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So I turn one arrow round so both copies of $c$ agree… and they glue into a square.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The square’s orange sides are both $a$, its blue sides both $b$. Glue them, arrows matching…

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: …and it’s a torus: one vertex, three edges $a$, $b$, $c$, and two triangles.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Turn one blue arrow round. Same pieces, glued differently: a Klein bottle.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: It only crosses itself because we’re drawing it in 3D.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Twist both pairs for $ℝP²$, and a triangle’s arrows run in a circle. No first corner: not a simplex.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Turning $c$ just moves the problem. Turn a whole blue pair: two vertices.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the yard: click an arrow with the Cell Hammer (2) to turn it round, then click the gold press to fold.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Triangles with ordered corners, glued in order. That’s a Δ-complex.

videos.title: The Boundary Blade

videos.synopsis: Chains are sums of simplices; the boundary drops each vertex with alternating signs; shared edges cancel; the boundary of a boundary is zero; homology keeps the cycles that are not boundaries.

scenes.description: The chain 2[v0v1] − [v1v2] lit on a square of edges.

scenes.title: Boundary of a triangle
scenes.description: One triangle is cut: two edges +1, one −1.

scenes.description: Four triangles round v4 with +1; two spokes are left at ±2 until [v0v3v4] turns to −1; only the rim is left.
The rim edges are cut one by one; every vertex total returns to zero.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A chain is a sum of edges, or of triangles, with whole numbers in front: $2[v₀v₁] − [v₁v₂]$ here.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Chains add like vectors. Hatcher calls the group of $n$-chains $Δₙ(X)$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The boundary drops one vertex at a time, with alternating signs: $∂[v₀v₁v₂] = [v₁v₂] − [v₀v₂] + [v₀v₁]$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: The minus is the edge I walk backwards going round.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Add triangles and their boundaries add too. Each inside edge gets counted twice…

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: …and cancels only with the right signs. $[v₀v₃v₄]$ runs the other way, so it gets $−1$. Left over: the rim.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now the boundary of that boundary. $∂[ab] = b − a$, end minus start, and each corner is entered once and left once.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Every time: $∂∂ = 0$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A chain with zero boundary is a cycle. Every boundary is one, like this loop round the filled tile.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: But the loop round the missing tile is a cycle that bounds nothing. $Hₙ$ = Ker ∂ / Im ∂ counts those: $H₁ ≅ ℤ$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the marsh: equip the Boundary Blade (7) and click a triangle or an edge to set its number.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Chains, their boundaries, and the holes left over. That’s simplicial homology.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A singular $n$-simplex is any continuous map $σ: Δⁿ → X$. For $n = 1$ that’s a path: smooth, wiggly, swinging wide.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Or one that never moves. No straight edges, no gluing to get right, so it works for every space.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The boundary formula is the same. For a path, $∂σ = σ(1) − σ(0)$: end minus start, however it bends.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: And the constant path ends where it starts: $p₃ − p₃ = 0$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Cycles work the same too. $α + β + γ + δ$ closes up, and it goes round the pond.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $γ − ε$ closes up as well. But a singular 2-simplex can fill the stone strip between them, so it’s a boundary.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Now bend a cycle. Push it however you like; it still goes round the pond once…

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: …because the bend sweeps out a filled strip. Homotopic maps induce the same map on homology: Theorem 2.10.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Squeeze the thick ring onto its middle circle. That’s a homotopy equivalence.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So the ring has the same homology as the circle: $H₁ ≅ ℤ$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the Shallows: the Blade (7) cuts paths and sets their numbers; the Tide Glass (3) bends and squeezes.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Any simplex will do, and bending never changes the count.

videos.title: Chase Scene
videos.plays: World 2 · Level 4 lesson, in Chase Channels
videos.synopsis: Exactness means image in equals kernel out; a short exact sequence; relative homology and the long exact sequence of a pair, used to find H₂(D², S¹) ≅ ℤ.

scenes.title: Exact
scenes.description: A row of locks ℤ₄ → ℤ₄ → ℤ₂; gold rings mark what arrives, blue tiles what drains to 0.

scenes.title: Try the sluice
scenes.description: The left sluice tries 1 ↦ 0, 1 ↦ 1, then 1 ↦ 2, which is exact.

scenes.title: Short exact
scenes.description: 0 → ℤ₂ → ℤ₄ → ℤ₂ → 0: both sluices set; all locks green.

scenes.title: A pair
scenes.description: The disk and its rim beside a row of four locks, one unknown.

scenes.title: The disk and its rim
scenes.description: The unknown lock tries 0, ℤ₂, then ℤ, and the row turns green.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Blade on sluices and unknown locks.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A row of groups is exact at a group when what the map in delivers is exactly what the map out kills.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Gold rings show what arrives from the left. Blue tiles are what the right-hand sluice drains to $0$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Send $1$ to $0$ and only $0$ arrives. Send $1$ to $1$ and everything arrives. Neither matches the blue.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Send $1$ to $2$: gold on blue. Exact!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Zeros at both ends, $0 → A → B → C → 0$, make a short exact sequence. $A$ goes in one-to-one; $B$ maps onto $C$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Here $ℤ₂$ sits inside $ℤ₄$ as the even tiles, and what’s left over is $ℤ₂$ again.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Relative homology $Hₙ(X, A)$ counts chains in $X$ but treats anything inside $A$ as zero.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Every pair gives a long exact sequence: $… → Hₙ(A) → Hₙ(X) → Hₙ(X, A) → Hₙ₋₁(A) → …$

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: For the disk and its rim, $H₂(D², S¹)$ sits between two zeros, so $∂$ is an isomorphism onto $H₁(S¹) ≅ ℤ$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: The whole disk, and its boundary is the rim!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the Channels: click a sluice with the Blade (7) to change where it sends $1$, or an unknown lock to try a group.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In from the left equals drained to zero on the right, all along the row. Exact sequences.

videos.title: Cut and Paste
videos.plays: World 2 · Level 5 lesson, in Excision Cut
videos.synopsis: Relative homology of a pair; excision lets you cut away anything whose closure lies in the interior of A; good pairs give H(X, A) ≅ H̃(X/A); climbing the pairs (Dⁿ, Sⁿ⁻¹) computes the homology of spheres.

scenes.title: A pair
scenes.description: A disk X with a blue collar A round its rim.

scenes.title: Excision
scenes.description: Three holes are cut deep inside the collar.

scenes.title: Too close to the edge
scenes.description: Four marked regions; a and b are cut, c and d stay.

scenes.title: Good pairs
scenes.description: The disk’s rim is crushed to a point and the disk closes into a sphere.

scenes.title: The ladder
scenes.description: A grid of H̃ᵢ(Sⁿ) pads lights its diagonal, one rung at a time.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Blade and Suspension Sling.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A pair $(X, A)$: here $X$ is a disk and $A$ the blue collar round its rim. $Hₙ(X, A)$ treats everything in $A$ as zero.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So cutting part of $A$ away ought to change nothing. Excision says it doesn’t, with one condition.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: If the closure of $Z$ lies in the interior of $A$, then $H(X − Z, A − Z) ≅ H(X, A)$. That’s Theorem 2.20.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So no cutting right up against the collar’s inner edge.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A region that pokes out of $A$ can’t go. Nor can $A$ itself: its closure touches its own inner edge.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Regions $a$ and $b$ sit strictly inside the collar. Those can be excised.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: For a good pair, $Hₙ(X, A) ≅ H̃ₙ(X/A)$: crush all of $A$ to a single point.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Crush the disk’s rim and it closes into a sphere: $H₂(D², S¹) ≅ H̃₂(S²)$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The pair $(Dⁿ, Sⁿ⁻¹)$ gives $H̃ᵢ(Sⁿ) ≅ H̃ᵢ₋₁(Sⁿ⁻¹)$. Start from two points, $S⁰$, and climb.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: One lit pad per row: $H̃ᵢ(Sⁿ)$ is $ℤ$ when $i = n$, and $0$ otherwise.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the Cut: the Blade (7) cuts regions and lights ladder pads; the Suspension Sling (4) crushes $A$ to a point.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Cut deep, crush, climb. Excision, and the homology of spheres.

videos.title: The Third Degree
videos.plays: World 2 · Level 6 lesson, in Dynamo Gate
videos.synopsis: The degree of a sphere map; homotopy invariance; z ↦ zᵏ has degree k and degrees multiply; reflections have degree −1, so the antipodal map has degree (−1)ⁿ⁺¹; hence S² cannot be combed.

scenes.title: Degree
scenes.description: A band wound on and back round a post; a pink marker line.

scenes.title: Homotopy invariance
scenes.description: The band is pulled tight, one backtrack at a time: two turns.

scenes.title: Composing
scenes.description: Two lever maps z^a and z^b; the composite band winds 2, then −2, then −6 times.

scenes.title: The antipodal map
scenes.description: A sphere with P; three mirrors switch on and f(P) lands on −P.

scenes.title: The hairy ball
scenes.description: A combed sphere; the comb turns three times, and two calm spots always remain.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Degree Dial.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A map $f: Sⁿ → Sⁿ$ sends $Hₙ(Sⁿ) ≅ ℤ$ to itself, so it can only multiply by a whole number: its degree.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: For a circle, that’s how many times the map winds round. Backward turns count as minus.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Pulling the band tight is a homotopy, and homotopic maps have the same degree. Here it’s $2$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Every turn back cancels a turn forward.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $z ↦ zᵏ$ has degree $k$, and composing multiplies degrees: deg$(f ∘ g)$ = deg $f$ · deg $g$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $z⁻³$ winds three times backwards, degree $−3$. Follow it with $z²$ and you get $2 × (−3) = −6$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The antipodal map sends each point straight through the center. On $S²$ it’s three reflections…

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: …so its degree is $(−1)³ = −1$. On $Sⁿ$ it’s $(−1)ⁿ⁺¹$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: If $S²$ could be combed, sliding along the hairs would turn the identity into the antipodal map…

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: …but $−1$ isn’t $1$. Theorem 2.28!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: At the Gate, the Degree Dial (8) tightens bands, sets powers, flips mirrors, and turns the comb.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: One whole number for every sphere map, and it settles a lot.

videos.title: Cell Block
videos.plays: World 2 · Level 7 lesson, in Cell Block
videos.synopsis: CW complexes are built skeleton by skeleton; the cellular boundary of a 2-cell is read off its rim word; this gives the homology of the torus, ℝP² and the Klein bottle; and the Euler characteristic counts the same from cells or from homology.

scenes.title: CW complexes
scenes.description: Crates attached in order: a point, two loops, then the 2-cell folds the torus.

scenes.title: Reading d₂
scenes.description: The torus square with its rim word; the Dial sets a and b to 0; the cell attaches.

scenes.title: ℝP²
scenes.description: A disk whose rim runs round a twice; the Dial reads 2.

scenes.title: Klein bottle
scenes.description: The square with one pair turned; the Dial reads a = 0, b = 2.

scenes.title: Euler characteristic
scenes.description: The Klein bottle folded; cells and ranks compared.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Cell-Smith and Degree Dial.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A CW complex is built a dimension at a time: points, then edges glued onto the points, then disks glued along their rims.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The torus takes four cells: one point, two loops $a$ and $b$, and one disk.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Cellular chains have one generator per cell. For $d₂$, walk once round the disk’s rim: $+1$ for each arrow with you, $−1$ against.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: The torus reads $a$, $b$, $a$ back, $b$ back. Zero and zero!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: For $ℝP²$, the disk’s rim runs round the one loop $a$ twice, the same way: $d₂ = 2a$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So $a$ is a cycle but $2a$ is a boundary: $H₁(ℝP²) = ℤ₂$. And $H₂ = 0$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The Klein bottle: turn one pair of arrows round. Now $a$ cancels, but $b$ counts twice.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $d₂ = 2b$, so $H₁ = ℤ ⊕ ℤ₂$ and $H₂ = 0$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Count cells with alternating signs and you get the Euler characteristic, $χ$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: And the ranks of homology give the same number: $1 − 2 + 1 = 1 − 1 + 0$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the Block: the Cell Hammer (2) attaches cells; the Degree Dial (8) sets each letter in $d₂$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Fewer pieces, the same holes. That’s cellular homology.

videos.title: Patchwork
videos.plays: World 2 · Level 8 lesson, in Patchwork Fields
videos.synopsis: The Mayer–Vietoris sequence computes a space from two patches and their overlap: the sphere from two caps, the circle from two arcs, the Klein bottle from two Möbius bands, the torus from two annuli.

scenes.title: Mayer–Vietoris
scenes.description: Two caps clasped onto a sphere.

scenes.title: The sphere
scenes.description: The row finds H₂(S²) = ℤ.

scenes.title: The circle
scenes.description: Two arcs cover a circle; their overlap is two pieces; the row finds H₁(S¹) = ℤ.

scenes.title: The Klein bottle
scenes.description: Two Möbius bands; the row finds ℤ ⊕ ℤ₂.

scenes.title: The torus
scenes.description: Two annuli; the row finds ℤ².

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Clasp and Blade.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Mayer–Vietoris: $… → Hₙ(A∩B) → Hₙ(A) ⊕ Hₙ(B) → Hₙ(X) → Hₙ₋₁(A∩B) → …$ is exact.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: It needs the interiors of $A$ and $B$ to cover $X$. Pick patches you understand; exactness does the rest.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Two caps cover the sphere. Each cap is a disk, with no holes; their overlap is a band — a circle.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So $H₂(S²)$ sits between zeros and matches $H₁$ of the circle: $ℤ$!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A circle from two arcs. Neither arc has a hole — but their overlap falls into two pieces.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $H₁(S¹)$ is the kernel of $ℤ² → ℤ²$, $(x, y) ↦ (x+y, x+y)$: one copy of $ℤ$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The Klein bottle is two Möbius bands glued along their edge — a circle that runs twice round each band.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So $H₁ = ℤ² / ⟨(2, −2)⟩ ≅ ℤ ⊕ ℤ₂$, and $H₂ = 0$. That’s Hatcher’s Example 2.47.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The torus from two annuli: one loop comes from each side of $∂$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: $H₁(T) = ℤ²$ — round the tube, and round the ring.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the Fields: clasp patches on with the Van Kampen Clasp (5), and try groups in the unknown lock with the Blade (7).

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Two patches and their overlap. That’s Mayer–Vietoris.

videos.title: Mod Squad
videos.plays: World 2 · Level 9 lesson, in Mod Mill
videos.synopsis: Homology with coefficients; over ℤ₂ signs vanish, so ℝP² and the Klein bottle get H₂ = ℤ₂; over ℤ, H₂ of a closed surface detects orientability.

scenes.title: Coefficients
scenes.description: The fan of four triangles, coefficients now 0 or 1.

scenes.title: No signs
scenes.description: All four triangles set to 1; only the rim is left.

scenes.title: ℝP² mod 2
scenes.description: ℝP²’s 2-cell: the coefficient reads 0 mod 2 and the cell folds up.

scenes.title: Klein mod 2
scenes.description: The Klein bottle’s 2-cell: both letters 0 mod 2.

scenes.title: Orientable?
scenes.description: Four surfaces sorted into orientable and non-orientable bins.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: The Blade.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Homology with coefficients uses chains $Σ gᵢσᵢ$ with each $gᵢ$ in a group $G$. Same boundary formula, new arithmetic.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Take $G = ℤ₂$: every coefficient is $0$ or $1$, and $1 + 1 = 0$. So $−1 = 1$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In Cancel Marsh one triangle needed $−1$. Mod 2, set all four to $1$ and each inside edge gets $1 + 1 = 0$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: No more checking which way round a triangle goes!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $ℝP²$: over $ℤ$, $d₂ = 2a$. Mod 2, that’s $0$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: So the disk becomes a cycle: $H₂(ℝP²; ℤ₂) = ℤ₂$, though $H₂(ℝP²) = 0$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: The Klein bottle: $a$ cancels, $b$ counts twice — and twice is $0$ mod 2.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $H₂(K; ℤ₂) = ℤ₂$. Mod 2, a flip can’t cancel anything.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Over $ℤ$, a closed surface has $H₂ = ℤ$ exactly when it’s orientable (Chapter 3).

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Sphere and torus: yes. $ℝP²$ and Klein: no. And mod 2, they all look alike.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In the Mill, the Blade (7) does it all: flip a coefficient between $0$ and $1$, attach a cell, sort a surface.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Same cells, new arithmetic, and different holes come into view.

videos.title: Forget the Order
videos.plays: World 2 · Level 10 lesson, in Abelian Ford
videos.synopsis: Loops are 1-cycles, giving π₁ → H₁; in H₁ the order of a loop’s letters is forgotten, so commutators die and totals survive: H₁ ≅ π₁ abelianized (Theorem 2A.1).

scenes.title: Loops as words
scenes.description: A word of letter tiles across the ford.

scenes.title: Forget the order
scenes.description: a b a⁻¹ a b: a swap, a cancellation, a swap — a b².

scenes.title: Commutators die
scenes.description: a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹ dissolves completely.

scenes.title: Totals survive
scenes.description: b a a b⁻¹ reduces to a².

scenes.title: Theorem 2A.1
scenes.description: The Commutator’s word dissolves.

scenes.title: How to play
scenes.description: Clasp and Blade.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Summary card; title card.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In $π₁$ a loop is a word in $a$, $b$ and inverses. The only move: cancel a letter against its inverse beside it.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: But a loop is also a 1-cycle, so it has a class in $H₁$. What does $H₁$ keep?

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: In $H₁$ neighbours may swap places. Swap, cancel, swap: $a b a⁻¹ a b$ becomes $a b²$.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: Only the totals are left: once round $a$, twice round $b$.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: A commutator, $aba⁻¹b⁻¹$, is a real loop in $π₁$ of the figure-eight. It never cancels there.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Forget the order and it’s gone: its totals are zero.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: $b a a b⁻¹$: swapping and canceling never change totals, so $a²$ survives.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Forgetting the order isn’t forgetting everything.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Theorem 2A.1: $π₁ → H₁$ is onto, and its kernel is the commutator subgroup.

captions.speaker: Gyroid
captions.text: So $H₁$ is $π₁$ abelianized. Even the Commutator’s own word dissolves!

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: At the Ford: the Clasp (5) swaps neighbours; the Blade (7) cancels a letter with its inverse.

captions.speaker: Emmy Boundary
captions.text: Keep the totals, forget the order: $H₁ ≅ π₁$ abelianized.
